chief_complaint: Extensive, painful verrucous skin lesions on his left foot and lower leg, with acute pain and swelling for the past three days.
history_of_present_illness: The patient's condition began ten years prior following a leech bite on the dorsum of his left foot. A week later, a small painless red nodule developed at the site. Over the following years, the lesion slowly increased in size, with further lesions developing and spreading up to his knee. Three days before admission, his ankle became acutely painful and swollen. The lesions are described as cauliflower-like masses and oval plaques, which are partly erythematous, fungating, purulent, and produce a bad odor.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a farmer residing in northern Laos. The initial lesion developed at the site of a leech bite ten years ago.
vitals: Vital signs were normal and the patient was afebrile upon presentation.
physical_exam: The left lower leg and foot were grossly swollen, with hyperaemic and hot skin. There were several cauliflower-like masses and oval plaque-like lesions on his left lower leg and foot. The lesions were partly erythematous, fungating, and purulent, with an associated bad odour.
labs_and_diagnostics: Radiography of the left leg and foot showed no bone involvement. Direct microscopy of wet film scrapings from the lesions revealed characteristic brownish, round, thick-walled, multiseptate sclerotic cells typical of chromoblastomycosis. A bacterial culture of the pus grew Escherichia coli. PCR from skin tissue was positive, and sequencing showed 100% similarity with Fonsecaea pedrosoi, F. monophora, and F. nubica.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnoses for the chronic verrucous skin lesions included other fungal infections like sporotrichosis and mycetoma, as well as mycobacterial infections such as cutaneous tuberculosis and leprosy. Non-infectious causes like squamous cell carcinoma and sarcoidosis were also considered. The acute inflammatory signs suggested a possible bacterial superinfection or deep vein thrombosis.
management_and_clinical_course: A secondary bacterial superinfection was suspected and treated with local iodine-based antiseptics and oral antibiotics, which were changed to co-trimoxazole based on culture results showing Escherichia coli. Antifungal treatment was initiated with itraconazole pulse therapy (400mg/d for 7 days monthly), along with surgical debridement of all lesions. Oral terbinafine was later added for 9 months, supplemented with local terbinafine ointment for 6 months. Liver function was monitored and remained normal. The lesions healed uneventfully, with some residual swelling and hypopigmentation.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was chromoblastomycosis, complicated by a secondary bacterial superinfection. The fungal diagnosis was confirmed by direct microscopy of skin scrapings showing characteristic sclerotic cells (Medlar bodies) and by positive PCR from skin tissue, with sequencing identifying a Fonsecaea species (F. pedrosoi, F. monophora, or F. nubica). The bacterial superinfection was confirmed by a pus culture growing Escherichia coli.
